unit.title: School Life & Schedules: Ordinals, Subjects, and Time

lesson.title: Design Your Dream Schedule and Defend One Choice
lesson.subject: spanish

contentBlocks.text: This week you learned school words, the ordinal numbers, the interesante / aburrido split, and how to say when a class meets. Today you use all of it to build your own horario ideal — a dream schedule — and then stand up and defend one choice in Spanish.

Make a schedule with six periods and one descanso. For each period write the ordinal, the time, and the materia:

- Primer periodo: a las nueve — arte
- Segundo periodo: a las diez — música
- Tercer periodo: a las once — educación física
- Descanso: a las doce
- Cuarto periodo: a la una — ciencias
- Quinto periodo: a las dos — español
- Sexto periodo: a las tres — historia

Notice the ordinals doing their jobs: primer periodo and tercer periodo drop the -o (masculine singular noun right after), but segundo and cuarto stay whole.

You choose the start time, the order, and how much tarea your dream classes give.

Pick one choice from your schedule and defend it out loud, in three or four sentences. Use this shape:

1. What and when: Tengo arte en el primer periodo, a las nueve.
2. Why, with interesante or aburrido: Es mi materia favorita porque es muy interesante y dibujamos todos los días.
3. A contrast with pero: Las matemáticas son un poco aburridas para mí, pero el arte nunca es aburrido.
4. One more reason: Además, no hay mucha tarea en la clase de arte.

Check every adjective: interesante does not change; aburrido matches its subject.

Two words worth a note:

- el descanso and el recreo both mean the school break. el recreo is the more common word in many Latin American schools, especially for younger grades; el descanso is understood everywhere and also just means 'a rest.'
- el horario means a schedule of any kind — a class schedule, a bus schedule, a store's hours. La tienda tiene un horario de nueve a seis.

And remember the false split from Day 3: es aburrido describes the class; estoy aburrido describes how a person feels.

You designed a schedule and argued for part of it in Spanish, using this week's whole toolkit. Take the mini-quiz to close the week. Next week: -ar verbs — one ending pattern that unlocks hundreds of verbs like hablar, estudiar, and trabajar.

objectives: Design a six-period dream schedule in Spanish, labeling each period with an agreeing ordinal (primer/segundo/tercer periodo...) and a start time (a la(s) + hour)
Defend one scheduling choice aloud in three or four sentences using interesante / aburrido with correct agreement, a pero contrast, and a porque reason
Demonstrate week-6 vocabulary, the primero -> primer rule, and interesante/aburrido agreement on the mini-quiz
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Recap the week: school words, ordinals + the primer/tercer shortening, interesante vs. aburrido, a la(s) + hour.
2. Model a dream schedule on the board — six periods, one descanso, an ordinal and a time on each line. Think aloud about the primer/tercer shortening as you write.
3. Students build their own horario ideal on the worksheet grid.
4. Model the four-sentence defense with your own example, then have students draft theirs.
5. Students present their one defended choice to the class or in small groups; listeners ask one follow-up question (¿A qué hora...? / ¿Por qué...?).
6. Administer the mini-quiz (quiz-spanish-6-6-5).
7. Complete the worksheet reflection.
8. Preview next week: -ar verbs.
differentiationTips: Struggling: provide the schedule grid pre-labeled with ordinals and times so the student only fills in subjects, and give the four defense sentences as fill-in-the-blank frames
Ready for more: have them write the full defense as a short paragraph and add a second defended choice with a different reason
If the mini-quiz shows a gap — usually the primero -> primer rule or interesante taking a false '-a' ending — revisit Day 1's or Day 3's grammar block before starting week 7
teacherGuide.answerKey: Schedules vary. A complete schedule has six periods plus a descanso, each period labeled with an ordinal that agrees (primer/tercer periodo shortened; segundo/cuarto/quinto/sexto whole) and a time with a la(s). A complete defense has: what + when, a why using interesante or aburrido (agreeing correctly), a pero contrast, and one more reason. Usage notes: el descanso / el recreo both = the break; el horario = any schedule; es aburrido (the class) vs. estoy aburrido (the person). Mini-quiz answers are in quiz-spanish-6-6-5.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Closes week 6's WA-WL-2015.1.2 arc with the scope-and-sequence Day 5 design — design a dream schedule and defend one choice to the class — turning the week's reading and vocabulary into a presentational performance. The defense frame recycles pero and the description structure from week 5 and sets up the sustained sentence-level output the -ar verb weeks build on. The mini-quiz is the week's mastery check on vocabulary, the ordinal apócope, and interesante/aburrido agreement.

worksheet.title: Design Your Dream Schedule and Defend One Choice

generationData.instructions: Design your horario ideal, then defend one choice in Spanish.

rows.problem: Build a six-period dream schedule. For each period write the ordinal (primer periodo, segundo periodo...), the time (a la(s) + hour), and the materia. Add one descanso.
Circle the ordinals in your schedule. Which ones dropped the -o, and why?
Pick one class. Write one sentence saying what it is and when, and one sentence saying why, using interesante or aburrido with the correct ending.
Write your full 3-4 sentence defense: what + when, why (interesante/aburrido + porque), a pero contrast, and one more reason.
Reflection: what was the most useful thing you learned this week about reading a Spanish schedule?
